procedural_history.originating_court: The case originated with a petition filed directly in the Supreme Court of India under Article 32 of the Constitution.
procedural_history.impugned_order: The initial petition challenged the detention order dated August 29, 1968, made under section 3(1)(a)(ii) of the Preventive Detention Act.  Later, the petition was amended to also challenge a fresh detention order dated August 28, 1969, issued under the same section of the Act.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: There were no High Court proceedings mentioned in the text. The case went directly to the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court initially granted time to the State of Assam to provide full material related to the first detention order. However, before the next hearing, a new detention order was issued. The petitioner then amended his petition to challenge the new order as well. The Supreme Court ultimately allowed the petition and ordered the petitioner to be set at liberty, finding the detention order dated August 28, 1969, to be invalid under section 13(2) of the Preventive Detention Act.

directions: The petitioner shall be set at liberty forthwith.

issue.issue_text: Whether a fresh order of detention under Section 13(2) of the Act is valid if it is based on facts that arose during the period of the previous detention, rather than on fresh facts that have arisen after the expiry of that detention period.

facts: A petitioner was under a detention order that was set to expire on August 29, 1969.
A fresh detention order was issued against him on August 28, 1969, one day before the previous order expired.
The grounds for this new order were based on facts that allegedly occurred during the period of the previous detention, such as maintaining links with associates while in custody.
law: Section 13(2) of the Preventive Detention Act states that a fresh detention order can be made against the same person after the revocation or expiry of a previous order only if it is based on "fresh facts" that have arisen "after the date of revocation or expiry."
The Court interprets this to mean that facts that arise *during* a period of detention are not sufficient grounds for a new order under this section.
application: The Court noted that the new detention order was issued on August 28, a day *before* the previous order expired.
Therefore, it was logically impossible for the new order to be based on facts that had arisen *after* the expiry of the previous detention, as required by Section 13(2).
Even if the alleged facts (maintaining links while in custody) were true, they occurred *during* the previous detention period, not after its expiry.
As a result, these facts did not satisfy the legal requirement for issuing a fresh detention order under Section 13(2).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the fresh detention order was not justified under Section 13(2) of the Act because it was not based on fresh facts that arose after the expiry of the previous detention. The order was therefore invalid, and the detention under it was illegal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a fresh order of detention under Section 13(2) of the Act is valid if it is based on facts that arose during the period of the previous detention, rather than on fresh facts that have arisen after the expiry of that detention period.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner challenged the validity of the new detention order (dated August 28, 1969), arguing it was illegal. The grounds for this new order were identical to the previous one and it was issued before the prior detention period had expired, which is a violation of the Act.
respondent_arguments: The text does not explicitly state the respondent's legal arguments. It only mentions that the respondent (State of Assam) issued a fresh detention order and requested more time from the court to gather materials to justify it, but failed to do so.

cases.case_name: Hadibandhu Das v. District Magistrate, Cuttack and Another
cases.principle: A fresh detention order can be made on the revocation or expiry of a previous detention order only in cases where fresh facts have arisen after the date of revocation or expiry.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A fresh detention order can be made upon the revocation or expiry of a previous detention order only in cases where fresh facts have arisen after the date of revocation or expiry. Facts that arise during the period of the previous detention are not considered fresh facts for this purpose.
obiter: Detention of a person without trial, even for a single day, is a matter of great consequence.

If a person in preventive custody was able to maintain links with associates, it casts a sad reflection on the persons in charge of him while he was in custody and it would appear that his detention could serve no useful purpose.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A fresh order of detention under Section 13(2) of the Act is invalid if it is based on facts that arose during the period of the previous detention. The law requires that a fresh order must be made on fresh facts which have arisen after the date of the previous order's expiry. In this case, the new order was passed a day before the expiry of the old one, and the additional ground cited—that the petitioner maintained links with associates while in custody—related to the period of detention itself, not to any facts arising after its expiry. Therefore, the order was not justified under the Act.
legal_tests_applied: Under s. 13(2) what is required is that fresh facts should have arisen after the expiry of the previous detention. Facts arising during the period of detention are, therefore, not relevant when applying the provisions of s. 13(2).
